b: For many anglers, that’s a common refrain at the end of a fishing trip.
For David Shaw, it had deeper meaning on a hot summer evening at Smithville Lake in northwest Missouri.
He was dying of cancer when he joined his son Tyler for what he sensed would be the last cast of his illustrious career.
David Shaw liked traveling to the Northland to fish for big smallmouth bass. Photo courtesy of Tyler Shaw.
The father-son duo had dominated local and regional bass tournaments at Smithville Lake for some time. Now they were back for David, 76, to say goodbye.
“It was pretty emotional,” David told Wired2fish just days before he passed away on Nov. 11. “But it was something I wanted to do.”
Weak and exhausted by the cancer treatments, David was only able to fish for 45 minutes of the three-hour Livin2Fish evening bass tournament held this past summer. But he didn’t want to go in early.

“We went back to places Dad had fished since the lake first came in: old stumps that were still there, ridges with brush on them, off-shore structure,” Tyler recalled. “And he caught fish. He caught a keeper and three shorts in the 45 minutes he fished until he just couldn’t cast anymore.
“Then he just sat back and took everything in.”
The Shaws finished just out of the money in the local tournament, but they went home with something far more significant than a trophy: memories.
Tyler tears up remembering that special fishing trip.
“I think everyone knew that it was just a matter of time,” said Tyler, 42, who lives at Lake Waukomis, Missouri. “I was lucky enough to have one more day in the boat with him.”
David (left) and Tyler Shaw pose with two of the many trophies they won in bass tournaments at Smithville Lake. Photo courtesy of Tyler Shaw.
Every well-known bass lake has a local legend. David Shaw filled that role at Smithville Lake.
Few dominated the tournament scene at the Kansas City area-reservoir the way Shaw and his son did when Smithville was still in its heyday
One year, the father-son team finished third or better in 15 of the 20 Thursday night buddy events sponsored by Burton’s Bait and Tackle.

“When the Shaws would show up for a tournament, most of the guys would say, ‘We’re fishing for second (place) tonight.’ They were that good,” said Gary Burton, who ran the tournaments and became a close friend of David Shaw.
Burton constantly got a reminder of just how good the Shaws were. He remembers one evening tournament when he caught his personal-best bass, a fish weighing 8.5 pounds.
“I thought for sure that I would win big bass,” Burton said. “Then David came in with one that weighed 8.86 pounds.”
Tyler credited his dad’s success to an intimate knowledge of what’s beneath the surface of the 7,190-acre reservoir.

“He fished the lake before it even filled,” Tyler said. “He and some of his friends would drag aluminum boats down to different spots, and he learned what the creeks, fence rows, humps, and dropoffs looked like before they were even flooded.”
Shaw also got a sense of how the bass would react to different types of weather, their travel patterns and the isolated cover that consistently held fish.
“In that last tournament we fished, he caught a bass in a place he had fished since the lake filled,” Tyler said.
The father-son team found much of their success at some of that off-shore structure.
“That was our bread and butter,” David said. “While others were pounding the banks, we were out there fishing structure.”
The duo succeeded by playing off each other’s strengths.

“My dad loved to use a Senko. He would use it Texas rigged and add just enough weight to get it down,” Tyler said. “I would use a bigger bait like a big Brush Hog and we’d give the fish two different looks.”
David’s success went beyond Smithville Lake, though.

He fished regional circuits and did well at Truman, Bull Shoals, and Table Rock reservoirs, among others. He became the face of Heartland Trails as the emcee of the circuit’s tournaments, and he was a familiar and respected figure among regional anglers.
The elder Shaw later guided primarily for walleyes at Smithville, and often traveled to northern climes in search of trophy smallmouth bass.

Even when he was fighting cancer, he and Tyler competed in tournaments and won championships. He was first diagnosed with neck and head cancer in 2018. That started a long stretch of peaks and valleys of health problems. David contracted COVID in 2020; after recovering from that, he developed a blood disorder. Complications from that ultimately proved too much to overcome.
Now, Tyler looks back at a lifetime of special moments in the boat with a dad who taught him that there was more to bass fishing than the catch.
“I’ll really miss him,” Tyler said. “But I’m glad he’s not in pain anymore. He’s in a better place now.”
